articles.title: Who is Eric Deters? The MAGA donor Kimberly Guilfoyle sought $100K from for AmEx bill
articles.summary: Eric Deters, a former Kentucky congressional candidate and longtime ally of President Trump, has emerged in the national spotlight after an explosive report...
articles.body:
Eric Deters, a former Kentucky congressional candidate and longtime ally of President Trump, has emerged in the national spotlight after an explosive report revealed his alleged text exchanges with Kimberly Guilfoyle, U.S. ambassador to Greece, over her credit card debt.

The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that Guilfoyle, ex-wife of California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) and the former fiancé of Donald Trump Jr., allegedly pressed Deters to pay her $100,000 American Express balance without leaving a paper trail and, in exchange, promised to help him reach senior administration officials.

Deters, 63, is a former attorney, businessman and conservative radio host who has spent years building connections within Trump's inner circle. He declined to make the payment and has since publicly accused Guilfoyle of offering political access in exchange for large sums of money.

Guilfoyle's dealings with Deters began drawing attention after the Journal obtained hundreds of text messages, emails and letters, detailing their relationship in a bombshell report.

According to the outlet, Guilfoyle told Deters she needed the balance to be paid ahead of her July 9, 2025, confirmation hearing before the Senate.

"Honey please I need you to get this done for me today," she wrote in one exchange on the messaging app Signal, which was obtained by the Journal. The message was sent on July 3, 2025 — just days before her hearing.

She then reportedly sent Deters instructions to wire $100,000 directly to her American Express account, suggesting the payment would not leave a paper trail.

"It won't show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express," she wrote. "Please."

Deters refused, telling Guilfoyle he did not have the money and could not make the payment without jeopardizing his marriage.

The Journal also reported that Guilfoyle repeatedly urged Deters not to document their financial arrangements in writing, warning that doing so could threaten her ambassadorship.

In an interview with ABC's "Good Morning America" on Thursday, Deters characterized their relationship as a "quid pro quo," alleging that Guilfoyle promised to use her political connections to help him if he provided the money.

"She made it very clear, and the text messages make it very clear, she was so desperate for me to send that $100,000," Deters said, claiming Guilfoyle offered to become his "ride or die in the Trump world" if he paid her.

Guilfoyle's attorney has since disputed the authenticity of the messages without identifying specific inaccuracies, saying the ambassador was owed money for previous speaking engagements and travel expenses — a claim Deters denied.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio refused to comment on the story, telling reporters while on diplomatic travel in Greece that he does not know if the allegations are "true or not true."

"Our job is not to respond every time someone decides to give the media something without any advance warning, without having any chance to look at it and see what's in there," Rubio said.

Deters has been an outspoken supporter of Trump since he first campaigned for president in 2016, promoting Trump's candidacy as a morning radio host based in Ohio.

He frequently declared himself "Trump today, Trump tomorrow, Trump forever," according to the Journal.

His connections to Trump's family grew through Freedom Fest, a conservative gathering he launched in northern Kentucky in 2020 in opposition to COVID-19 mandates.

The event attracted prominent figures in Trump's inner circle, including the president's sons Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr., as well as Guilfoyle, who became engaged to Donald Trump Jr. that same year before the couple announced their split in 2024.

Deters told the Journal he paid Guilfoyle $300,000 over several years to speak at the event, along with $200,000 to Donald Trump Jr. and $100,000 to Eric Trump.

He also donated $125,000 to the MAGA Inc. super PAC, according to Federal Election Commission records.

The event continued for several years, though its 2026 edition was canceled after organizers sold just six of the 100 available VIP tickets, according to Deters. In September, he said on Facebook that he is "never ever, ever, ever ever doing this event again."

After Trump's 2024 election victory, Deters began seeking Guilfoyle's help with several disputes involving federal agencies.

One involved an Ohio spine surgeon named Abubakar Atiq Durrani, who fled to Pakistan after facing charges of performing unnecessary surgeries and defrauding insurance companies.

Deters, who said he was advising attorneys representing hundreds of Durrani's former patients, wanted the Justice Department to pursue his extradition.

He also sought assistance with an IRS inquiry into a tax deduction connected to the sale of his interest in the family business.

According to the Journal, Guilfoyle contacted then-IRS Commissioner Billy Long on Deters's behalf and discussed reaching other senior administration officials.

Deters also offered to pay her $1 million if she could arrange an interview with podcaster Tucker Carlson, hoping to draw attention to the Durrani case. The interview never materialized.

Deters told the Journal that despite his financial contributions and connections, Guilfoyle failed to deliver on her promises, which included lobbying top Trump officials such as FBI Director Kash Patel and former Attorney General Pam Bondi.

"She never came through on anything," he said.

Political career and legal controversies

Deters launched several unsuccessful bids for political office, including for Kentucky governor and Congress, where he challenged Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) in the state's 4th Congressional District.

The northern Kentucky businessman, who previously co-owned regional restaurant chain Snappy Tomato Pizza, is also a former criminal defense attorney.

His legal career was marked by repeated disciplinary proceedings. In 2020, Deters was banned from entering a courthouse in Hamilton County, Ohio, after threatening on social media to burn it down.

The Kentucky Bar Association also twice suspended him over misconduct, including making false statements in court proceedings and filing frivolous claims.

The Kentucky Supreme Court rejected his effort to regain his license to practice law in 2021, with the chief justice describing Deters's approach to practicing law as "anarchy."

"Deters' lack of self-awareness is utterly amazing," the opinion reads.

Deters has since retired from practicing law, describing himself to the Journal as a "legal outlaw."

articles.title: BJP may fine-tune caste equations from UP in Modi Cabinet rejig
articles.summary: BJP may reshuffle Modi Cabinet to revamp Uttar Pradesh representation, with Rajya Sabha exits of Hardeep Puri, BL Verma and caste balance focus.
articles.body: Lucknow: BJP’s decision to drop Union ministers Hardeep Singh Puri and BL Verma from the Rajya Sabha has stirred buzz over a likely overhaul of Uttar Pradesh’s representation in the Modi Cabinet, with the party weighing the chances of inducting new faces ahead of the Assembly elections.The induction of new faces from the state into the Union council of ministers could provide BJP the opportunity to balance caste representation, reward organisational work and reinforce its electoral narrative.At present, besides PM Narendra Modi, UP is represented by 10 Union ministers: Rajnath Singh, Hardeep Singh Puri, Jayant Chaudhary, Jitin Prasada, Pankaj Chaudhary, Anupriya Patel, SP Singh Baghel, Kirti Vardhan Singh, BL Verma and Kamlesh Paswan.With Puri and Verma set to exit the Rajya Sabha, BJP is already looking at a reshuffle of its ministerial representation from the state. Puri’s exit is notable because unlike most of the other ministers from UP, his political role has not been rooted in the state’s caste and electoral arithmetic.Verma, on the other hand, has been an important Lodh face in western Uttar Pradesh. Sources said the party is contemplating replacing Verma with a new Lodh face from UP.The reshuffle could acquire another dimension if Union minister of state for finance Pankaj Chaudhary is also relieved of his ministerial responsibility. A seven-term MP from Maharajganj, Chaudhary, a Kurmi, was appointed UP BJP president in Dec last year. His continuation in the Union Cabinet would mean that he continues to hold two significant responsibilities of minister as we all as heading the state party organisation.A decision to drop him from the ministry would underline BJP’s preference for “one person, one post”, while allowing Chaudhary to devote entirely to the party’s preparations for the UP elections.If Puri, Verma and Chaudhary all cease to be members of the Union council of ministers then UP’s representation would fall from 10 to seven. That reduction, however, is unlikely to be viewed merely as a numerical loss within the BJP. Party strategists see the reshuffle as an opportunity to reset the social composition of the Union ministry from UP.“The party will consider all equations including caste, region and emerging leadership whenever it effects a reshuffle in the Union Cabinet. It is an important call to be taken by the party’s leadership,” said UP BJP spokesperson Hero Bajpai.According to BJP sources, the party is considering members belonging to the Brahmin, Lodh and Pasi communities for possible induction into the Modi ministry.The proposed exercise fits into the BJP’s effort to finetune its social coalition in Uttar Pradesh. articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed once called Barack Obama's re-election "no victory" for progressives, complicating his upcoming campaign rally with the former president.
articles.body: Abdul El-Sayed once accused President Barack Obama of failing to deliver on the progressive campaign promises that he outlined in the 2008 presidential campaign, calling his election to a second term a kind of compromise for progressives. "I realize that I have little hope because there has been less change," El-Sayed wrote in a 2012 op-ed for HuffPost. "But I have to say now what I’ve been holding in throughout his campaign and what I think all of us have to admit: Obama was not the right choice — he just wasn’t the wrong one." The resurfaced comments, published just days after the 2012 presidential election, complicate the political picture for El-Sayed as he prepares to campaign with Obama later this month. The comments also raise questions about what El-Sayed’s ideals for the Democratic Party would have looked like in 2012, highlighting his past satisfaction with one of the Democratic Party's most prominent figures. DEMS' LEFTWARD LURCH GETS LEGS AS EL-SAYED'S MICHIGAN SENATE VICTORY SPARKS PARTY DEBATE In particular, El-Sayed’s 2012 op-ed criticized Obama’s international record and strikes on Pakistan and Yemen, an underperforming economy and, in his view, little to no change in being accepted as a Muslim American. "I feel no more dignified, no more accepted as cops throughout the country have usurped my right to walk the streets freely without fearing unjustified interference. Inequality has accelerated and the divide between the haves and have-nots in our country has never been starker," El-Sayed wrote. "At home our economy continues to stagnate; its victims are so many of my peers who had also invested in ‘hope and change’ four years ago, who cannot find meaningful work." Notably, he did confirm that he had voted for Obama in 2008 and 2012. MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE ABDUL EL-SAYED SAYS LEADERS MUST ADDRESS ‘UNPAID DEBTS’ TO BLACK COMMUNITIES He also asserted that Obama’s record, as disappointing as it had seemed to him, was still better than the outlook of the failed Republican presidential nominee Mitt Romney. Even so, El-Sayed said Obama fell short of the ideal he, as a progressive, would have chosen for the country. "We really like the idea of Obama… let’s be clear, for progressives who care about peace, prosperity, civil liberties and the future of our country, Obama’ reelection last night was no victory. It was the rock we chose over the hard place," El-Sayed wrote. In recent months, as El-Sayed waged his Senate campaign in Michigan, Obama did not endorse the progressive, staying out of a primary between him and Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich. Like Obama and other Democrats, El-Sayed has championed the growth of government as a way to address the country’s top issues. In addition to calling for lowering housing costs, he’s advocated for Medicare for all, opposes corporate tax carve-outs, and supports tuition-free access to higher education. Obama has still not issued an official endorsement even though he is slated to take the stage alongside El-Sayed on Oct. 24 for a rally with other Michigan Democrats. The former president highlighted the event in a post to social media on Monday. articles.title: El-Sayed on Trump calling him ‘Mohammed’ in latest attack: ‘He knows my name’
articles.summary: Michigan Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed (D) accused President Trump of using his Muslim faith against him after the commander in chief attacked the candidate Wednesday evening. In a Truth Social post, the president called the Democrat “Mohammed El-Sayed” and dubbed him a “RADICAL Extremist, Terrorist Sympathizer.” “He knows my name is Abdul. He says it…
articles.body:
Michigan Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed (D) accused President Trump of using his Muslim faith against him after the commander in chief attacked the candidate Wednesday evening.

In a Truth Social post , the president called the Democrat “Mohammed El-Sayed” and dubbed him a “RADICAL Extremist, Terrorist Sympathizer.”

“He knows my name is Abdul. He says it everyday,” the Democrat wrote on the social platform X on Thursday morning. “But he’s not just attacking me. He’s attacking all of us.”

“He thinks so low of us,” El-Sayed continued. “He thinks he can use my name and my faith to distract us from the suffering his policies are inflicting on us at the pump, at the grocery store, and at the doctor’s office. He thinks we don’t know any better. It’s time for change.”

El-Sayed, whose full name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, is Muslim and was born in Michigan to Egyptian immigrant parents. The progressive defeated centrist Rep. Haley Stevens (Mich.) in the state’s Democratic primary earlier this year.

The doctor and former director of the Wayne County Department of Health, Human and Veterans Services has campaigned on passing “Medicare for All.” Additionally, El-Sayed has proposed a hike in taxes on billionaires, banning PAC spending in politics and lowering everyday living costs.

Trump’s post came ahead of Michigan’s Senate debate on Thursday evening, in which El-Sayed and Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) will face off onstage for the first time. Trump has endorsed the Republican nominee in the race to succeed retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.).

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) also condemned the president’s Wednesday evening comment about El-Sayed.

“Abdul El-Sayed is on the road to being the next Senator from Michigan no matter how much bigoted bulls‑‑‑ a weak and desperate Donald Trump throws at him,” the Democratic leader wrote in an X post .

This is not the first time Trump has invoked El-Sayed’s faith and name in his attacks on the Democrat, nor is the Senate candidate alone in this treatment .

More broadly, Republicans this election cycle have warned of a takeover of “Sharia law” and a “massive Muslim takeover” if Democrats win the November elections — messaging critics say has platformed prejudice and hate against Muslim communities.

In an August Truth Social post , the president posted a photo of himself and his wife, first lady Melania Trump, alongside an image of El-Sayed and his wife. He wrote above, “Two VERY DIFFERENT America’s” and included the Democratic candidate’s full name in the post.

El-Sayed responded to the post in an interview with CNN’s Jake Tapper, saying Trump was “right” to point out a contrast between the two images.

“So yes, you’ve got two different visions of America,” he said. “Donald Trump’s vision is the one you’re living in right now. Can you afford gas? Can you afford your groceries? Do you believe, when you look your kids in the eye, that they’re going to have a better future than you did?”

articles.body: President Donald Trump lambasted incumbent Rep. Henry Cuellar, D-Texas, calling the congressman "a loser" on Wednesday, while criticizing the lawmaker for remaining a Democrat after receiving a presidential pardon. Trump pardoned Cuellar and his wife last year as the couple faced charges pertaining to bribery and money laundering. "In any event, I did the pardons, and made no deal, where a crooked politician would have, but I thought there would be a good chance that Cuellar, who was persecuted by Democrats because they didn’t like him, would have routinely gone over to the Republican Party — the people that saved him from years in prison," Trump wrote in a lengthy Truth Social post. HOUSE DEM BACK IN THE SPOTLIGHT AS BROTHER FACES UP TO 10 YEARS IN PRISON IF CONVICTED Cuellar, who has served in the U.S. House of Representatives since 2005, is currently seeking re-election. articles.body: More than 15 years after surviving several gunshot wounds during a terrorist attack at Fort Hood, retired Staff Sgt. Alonzo Lunsford is preparing to watch the man who shot him be executed. Speaking on "America’s Newsroom," Lunsford explained why he wants to attend the execution, which President Donald Trump recently approved to be carried out by firing squad. "You live by the sword, you die by the sword," Lunsford said. "And the way that he went about doing his deed was a coward's way because we didn't have any way to defend ourselves that day." TEXAS EXECUTES JAMAAL HOWARD DESPITE CONCERNS OVER LETHAL INJECTION DRUG USED IN FAILED TENNESSEE EXECUTION Trump approved the use of an Army firing squad to execute Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army major convicted of killing 13 people and wounding more than 30 others in the 2009 attack. Hasan opened fire on unarmed soldiers and civilians at Fort Hood while shouting "Allahu Akbar." Standing at 6-foot-9, Lunsford was shot several times, including once in the head. He believes attending the execution could bring closure to survivors and grieving families. "It's for two reasons. One is to give the families of the deceased a chance to close a chapter and also the survivors to close a chapter," Lunsford said of the execution. "And it sends a clear message that we will not stand for this activity in any of our armed services or in the United States," he added. Lunsford said that for him and others affected by the attack, even holidays are not the same, adding that families of the deceased will "never get a chance to cherish a Christmas, a Thanksgiving, an Easter" with their loved ones again. "For the survivors, even though we can still do those, celebrate those holidays, we still feel for those ones that we lost that day. Me personally, the holidays will never be the same for me. But what I can do for the ones that I lost that day is to live for them and to keep fighting so that we will never have this happen again," he added. TRUMP’S PENTAGON SHAKE-UP REVIVES A PRESIDENTIAL POWER PLAY WITH A LONG HISTORY Hasan remains on military death row at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas. If carried out, his execution would be the first by the U.S. military since 1961. The military last used a firing squad for an execution in 1945. Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell confirmed the decision on X, writing: "Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has recommended — and President Donald J. Trump has approved — death by U.S. Army firing squad for convicted terrorist Nidal Malik Hasan, the jihadist who opened fire on unarmed American soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009." ARMY IDENTIFIES 2 PILOTS KILLED IN APACHE HELICOPTER CRASH NEAR FORT HOOD DURING TRAINING EXERCISE Parnell added: "Judgment day for Hasan has finally come." articles.title: Homeland Security targets Democratic campaign after ICE arrest in Pennsylvania
articles.summary: Department of Homeland Security publicized the arrest of a Nigerian man for indecent exposure this week, it included a political attack that's drawing compla...
articles.body:
HARRISBURG, Pa. (AP) — When the U.S. Department of Homeland Security publicized the arrest of a Nigerian man for indecent exposure this week, it included a political attack that's drawing complaints from Democrats and a nonpartisan government watchdog.

The department's press release alleges that the man worked for a Democratic congressional candidate in a Pennsylvania battleground district, an unusual reference to a high-profile midterm contest.

"It's unbelievable that Janelle Stelson would employ an illegal alien to work on a congressional campaign, let alone a pervert who exposed himself in public," Charles Wall, deputy director for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, said in the press release.

A police report said the man had fliers for Stelson in his vehicle. Stelson's campaign denied that the man was an employee, and campaign finance reports don't show any payments to him.

The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to questions about how it established the man worked for Stelson. Its press release cited a news report quoting a conservative activist who asserted the connection.

Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington filed a complaint Thursday with the U.S. Office of Special Counsel, calling the department's attack on Stelson a blatant violation of the Hatch Act, which prohibits government officials from using their official positions to influence elections.

Donald Sherman, who leads CREW, said he'd never seen anything like the department's statement, where a law enforcement agency "goes out of its way" to reference a campaign affiliation in a press release that has nothing to do with election-related crimes.

The press release is "consistent with the message that the administration and that the president has sent from the top that ICE is to be involved in elections, regardless of what the law says," Sherman said.

Stelson, a former local television personality, is running for the second time against Republican Rep. Scott Perry in Pennsylvania's 10th Congressional District. It's expected to be one of the races that determines control of the U.S. House in the November midterms.

"If he is an illegal immigrant who committed a crime he should be deported," Stelson's campaign said. "We never heard of him prior to the news of his arrest. We are grateful to law enforcement for acting swiftly to arrest him."

President Donald Trump's administration is already under scrutiny for using federal resources for political purposes. The Department of Homeland Security has spent millions of taxpayer dollars on advertisements glorifying Trump and promoting his campaign messaging, drawing a pair of lawsuits and bipartisan backlash.

According to a police report obtained by The Associated Press, Chimaobim Adedayo Igbojekwe was arrested by an East Pennsboro Township police officer on Sept. 27 after a report of a suspicious vehicle parked next to a public park on a residential street in the Harrisburg suburb.

The officer wrote that, when Igbojekwe opened the door to talk to the officer, he noticed that Igbojekwe's "genitals were exposed."

Igbojekwe told the officer he was "in the neighborhood for work and that he was waiting to hand out flyers for Janelle Stelson's political campaign," according to the report. Igbojekwe produced a stack of flyers, the officer wrote.

It's not clear whether the man was working as a paid canvasser for another organization.

Igbojekwe was charged with disorderly conduct and indecent exposure. He pleaded guilty to disorderly conduct, court records say, and was later arrested by ICE.

Homeland Security said Igbojekwe entered the country legally in 2017 but remained past his "authorized period." He was granted deferred action by President Joe Biden's administration in 2021.

Igbojekwe's public defender did not return a call about the case.

Vance takes aim at Microsoft over foreign workers

Vice President Vance said Thursday that foreign workers at Microsoft will no longer be able to apply for permanent resident status in the U.S. through an employer-based program, after he accused the company of abusing the process.

The tech giant has been suspended from the permanent labor certification program , referred to as PERM, which allows companies to hire foreign workers to work permanently in the U.S.

“There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more than Microsoft,” Vance said at a press conference.

“Now, our message to Microsoft and to any other foreign or domestic corporation is quite simple,” he added. “We obviously want you to thrive in the United States of America.”

“We want people to invest in the United States of America, particularly the American technology sector. We are the biggest boosters of your industry. We want you to continue to grow and to employ a lot of people, but we want you to employ American workers.”

Vance accused Microsoft of benefiting heavily from both the PERM program and H-1B visa program last year, while also laying off thousands of American workers. The H-1B visa is used to hire international talent for specialty jobs.

Microsoft argued Thursday the “vast majority” of its employees in the U.S. are Americans, adding that 80 percent of its applications to the H-1B visa program last year were to extend or change the status of existing employees.

The company’s remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the U.S., it added.

“Microsoft only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category,” a spokesperson said in a statement.

“We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings. We pay our H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work.”

Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said Thursday that Adobe , Cognizant , Infosys and several other IT firms were also suspended from the PERM program.

articles.body:
President Trump lashed out at the media Thursday over its coverage on his comments suggesting Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego.

The president accused the media of reporting that he was “inviting” Iran to bomb the two California cities when he was talking about gas prices.

“What I was talking about was that a temporary increase in the price of Gasoline is a small price to pay for Iran not having a Nuclear Weapon and, if you want to see a big price, can you imagine what it would be like if they bombed San Diego and/or Los Angeles?” Trump wrote on Truth Social Thursday.

Trump went on to say he was making a comparison between “paying a little more, for a short time, for Gasoline, versus the bombing of our Major Cities.”

“Everybody knew that, the Fake News knew it as well, but they continue to go out and say that I am asking the enemy to bomb two Cities that I love,” he continued.

Trump first made the comments about bombing the two cities during a campaign rally in Nebraska on Monday, drawing immediately condemnation from California leaders.

The state’s Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) told The Hill on Tuesday that Trump was “mentally ill,” and called for the 25th Amendment to be invoked.

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass (D) called the comments “dangerous and could potentially compromise our safety,” while San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria (D) said in a statement the city was “not collateral damage.”

The White House also sought to push back on the characterization of the comments.

“The media freakout over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality,” White House communications director Steven Cheung wrote Tuesday on the social platform X.

Trump doubled down on the comments during a campaign rally in San Antonio on Wednesday but added he would not let Iran attack the American cities.

“You want to see some bad things happen? You want to see a country in free fall? We’re not going to let that happen,” he said.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) floated the idea of returning home to Louisiana if Republicans lose control of the House next year.

“Heaven forbid, if we lose this majority or whatever, I don’t know what my next chapter of life is,” Johnson told Fox News in an exclusive interview . “If God moves on our hearts and says we should, you know, go back to my hometown of Shreveport and start a lawn business, I’ll do that with equal fervor. I mean, I just want to be of my highest and best use to God and to my country.”

Johnson’s remarks come as Republicans confront a difficult political landscape marked by voter frustration over rising gas and grocery prices, President Trump’s low approval ratings and the historical headwinds facing the president’s party in the midterm elections. Decision Desk HQ forecasts that Democrats are favored to win back the House next year.

Johnson’s Speakership has often been rocky, marked by internal GOP fighting, a razor-thin margin and repeated challenges in keeping his conference unified behind the president’s agenda. The latest remarks represent perhaps the furthest Johnson has gone in publicly addressing his political future.

Asked about Johnson’s comments during a presser on Thursday, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said, “Well, he’ll ultimately have to make a decision about what comes next. I can say that the American people are about to retire Mike Johnson and the Republican majority in the House and possibly even in the Senate.”

Lance Trover, Johnson’s spokesperson, meanwhile, wrote on the social platform X that, “All the DC speculation about the Speaker because he dared to speculate about his potential future in the lawn care business is hilarious.”

“Not that I believe he’d be bad at it, but allowing it to overshadow the massive fundraising numbers announced this morning or the insane travel schedule he’s doing to keep the majority seems to be nothing short of trying to drive a contrived narrative,” he wrote.

Johnson also told Fox News he is going to be the Speaker in the next Congress, when asked whether he will run for minority leader if Republicans lose the House.

articles.title: A looming Social Security debate: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur dives into a Social Security debate that is particularly relevant for this year’s Senate candidates. Plus, Jonathan Allen examines the tricky position Democrats have put themselves in on corporate donations. — Adam Wollner Senate candidates run on raising Social Security taxes for higher incomes to prevent benefit cuts By Sahil Kapur A swath of Senate candidates across blue and red states are campaigning on raising Social Security taxes on higher incomes to prevent a benefit cut from taking effect in less than six years. Currently, Americans are taxed on earnings up to $184,500 to fund Social Security. These candidates, most of them Democrats, are calling for lifting that cap in order to boost revenues, ahead of a fast-approaching 2032 deadline for insolvency. Social Security is fully funded until the fourth quarter of 2032, according to its latest trustees report, after which benefits will automatically be cut by 22% — unless Congress takes action. The class of senators elected this fall will serve six-year terms ending January 2033, giving them power to address that deadline. In battleground Michigan, Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed said in a statement that if elected this fall, “I will end the cap on Social Security tax to make sure the rich pay their fair share. That way Social Security can last for decades to come.” He has called for nixing the cap in his official campaign platform. In red-leaning Iowa, Democrat Josh Turek supports eliminating the payroll tax cap, a spokesperson said, adding that if elected senator, he “will protect Social Security by lifting the cap to make billionaires pay their fair share.” And in the Republican stronghold of Texas, Democrat James Talarico is running on a platform to “ensure the wealthiest Americans pay their fair share into Social Security by eliminating the tax cap on those earning over $400,000 a year.” Talarico’s proposal points to an early disagreement among supporters of the idea: Should they eliminate the cap entirely or move the new tax threshold up to $400,000? Some lawmakers — including plenty of Democrats — have been politically sensitive about raising taxes on incomes below that amount. Read more → Democrats’ corporate PAC dilemma Analysis by Jonathan Allen Refusing campaign contributions from corporate PACs has become an article of faith among progressives. Setting aside for a moment the fact that corporate PACs can only give $5,000 per election directly to a candidate — hardly enough to influence races that turn on tens of millions of dollars — Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, showed why that pledge isn’t quite as straightforward as it seems in a Senate debate last night against Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek. Turek, she noted, is benefiting from massive ad buys by Democratic super PACs funded in large part by billionaires, corporations and dark money groups that don’t have to disclose their donors. In fact, the main Democratic vehicle backed by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Senate Majority PAC, had raised $150 million, much of it from those sources, through the end of June, the most recent reporting period. So, Hinson argued, Turek is misleading the public. “He is basically taking laundered corporate PAC money,” Hinson said. “If you don’t want to take that corporate PAC money, because that’s how it flows. It flows through people like Chuck Schumer, right to support you.” Turek ignored her invitation to call on corporate-funded outside groups to stop backing him. Her challenge could be posed to Democrats in every pivotal Senate and House race. Technically, super PACs can’t coordinate directly with campaigns, but they are designed to amplify candidates’ messages. Republicans do the same thing, and this year they are raising a lot more money to do it. Much of the public feels justified in wanting elected officials to be free of the binding ties that can be forged with political donations. That’s why so many Democratic candidates pat themselves on the back for refusing to take small direct contributions from corporate PACs, which are funded by employee donations. But how does a candidate turn his or her back on a super PAC that spends tens of millions of dollars — much more than the $5,000 from a direct corporate PAC contribution? And, when it comes to Schumer, a bogeyman of the Democrats’ left wing, how could they turn their backs on him after he raised all that money for them? Democratic voters may be surprised if Schumer wins a party leadership election next year after many candidates have tried to keep their distance from him. But they shouldn’t be. The election for minority leader or majority leader, depending on whether Democrats flip the Senate, will be conducted by secret ballot. Maybe they’ll reject Schumer like they reject corporate PAC donations. But don’t bet the super PAC on it. That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. articles.body:
Minnesota demands answers in Medicaid fraud fight with Trump

The Trump administration is escalating its Medicaid fraud fight against Minnesota , and state officials are bracing for hundreds of millions of dollars to be cancelled in the coming weeks.

Minnesota’s temporary human services commissioner and state Medicaid director John Connolly said the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) could officially withdraw up to $259 million in Medicaid payments that the Trump administration froze earlier this year.

CMS has already threatened to withhold Medicaid funding amounting to a $2 billion cut to the state, and it has frozen $550 million over the past several quarters because the administration said payments raised red flags for fraud. State officials are expecting to hear in the coming weeks if the first of the deferrals will result in a disallowance.

A disallowance is an official denial of federal Medicaid matching funds to a state for spending that doesn’t meet federal requirements.

The Trump administration has honed in on blue states ahead of the midterm elections, alleging massive Medicaid fraud and abuse. Administration officials have described red flags being raised over claims for providing care to deceased people, as well as allegedly billing for large numbers of patients at the same time.

At the time of the freeze over the summer, the administration said the funding is not being cut, but merely paused until state officials can provide more information to show that the “high-risk” Medicaid claims are justified .

But in a letter to CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz sent last week, Connolly asked to see the specific allegations .

“Minnesota has repeatedly asked CMS and federal law enforcement to provide evidence supporting public claims of fraud in Minnesota’s Medicaid program … to date, no evidence has been shared,” he wrote.

Connolly said the state is ready to take prompt action if and when the administration provides credible evidence.

articles.summary: A bipartisan group of dozens of lawmakers led by Rep. Steven Horsford (D-Nev.) and Sen. A letter from the group, sent to Google CEO Sundar Pichai and Spirit CEO Dave Davis, took issue with a proposed $10…
articles.body:
A bipartisan group of dozens of lawmakers led by Rep. Steven Horsford (D-Nev.) and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) is concerned over Google’s plan to acquire Spirit Airlines data to train its AI models.

A letter from the group , sent to Google CEO Sundar Pichai and Spirit CEO Dave Davis, took issue with a proposed $10 million sale of “Spirit Airlines’ internal data to Google for the purpose of training artificial intelligence systems,” which the lawmakers said they believed could violate “the privacy and confidentiality of thousands of current and former Spirit employees.”

The group of 119 lawmakers from both chambers continued the sale is “uncharted territory” as it would involve “approximately 100 million emails, 500 million Microsoft Teams messages, employee records, timecard records, payroll and tax information, and employment contracts.”

“We are concerned that conventional de-identification safeguards may not be sufficient to protect employee privacy in the context of modern artificial intelligence,” the lawmakers wrote, citing a National Institute of Standards and Technology report that stated in certain circumstances, de-identified data could be re-identified with the use of AI.

Google received the letter and had no interest in receiving personal information, according to a source familiar with the matter, adding that any data received will be rigorously de-identified by an independent third party.

“Innovation cannot come at the expense of workers’ privacy, and no employee data should move until real, enforceable safeguards are in place,” Horsford said in a press release Thursday.

A Google spokesperson told The Hill, “As we’ve said from the beginning of the process, we are not looking to buy any personal information from Spirit.”

“The information will either be completely excluded or will be deidentified by an independent third party before Google receives any data. We’re already working constructively with the appointed privacy ombudsman,” the spokesperson continued.

The lawmakers asked Google and Spirit to undertake six steps — such as excluding employee information as much as possible, establishing a de-identification protocol that affected employees agree to and protecting sensitive employee information when it is de-identified.

Worry has increased surrounding the development of AI models at major technology firms such as Google, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Anthropic. Leadership at all four companies were invited last week to the White House, where they agreed to a pledge to self-police AI development.

“Google’s focused on building the right way, with appropriate testing, evaluations, red-teaming, and other safeguards against misuse and misalignment – and releasing models or products only after they’ve been thoroughly reviewed,” Pichai wrote on social media after the pledge was announced.

Google also struck a deal with the Pentagon to provide its AI models for “any lawful governmental purpose,” a Pentagon official, told The Hill in April.

The deal received pushback from the company’s employees who felt that their “proximity to this technology creates a responsibility to highlight and prevent its most unethical and dangerous uses.”

articles.title: Pentagon says there will be a livestream of firing squad’s execution of the Fort Hood shooter
articles.summary: The execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan is scheduled for Dec. 3 in Texas.
articles.body: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Thursday the public would be able to watch the firing squad execution of a former Army officer convicted of a mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas. Speaking from the USS Abraham Lincoln to the conservative news outlet Real America’s Voice, Hegseth said Nidal Hasan is “going to get a firing squad of soldiers, and we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it.” “People need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” said Hegseth, who called the method of execution a “no-brainer.” Hegseth said the execution would be carried out at 1 p.m. Dec. 3 at Fort Hood — the same day of the week and time of day as Hasan’s attack. The execution will be livestreamed, according to a Defense Department official, though it’s not yet clear on which platform. The last military execution was in 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was hanged after he was convicted of raping and attempting to kill an 11-year-old girl in Austria. The last firing squad execution by the military was that of Pvt. Eddie Slovik in 1945 after he was court-martialed for desertion during World War II. Hasan was convicted of premeditated murder in 2013 through the Army court system and sentenced to death. Hasan, a former major and psychiatrist, opened fire at Fort Hood on Nov. 5, 2009, killing 13 people and wounding 32 others while shouting “Allahu akbar,” or “God is great” in Arabic. He was paralyzed from the waist down after he was shot during the attack, and he later told a panel of military mental health professionals that he wished he had been killed because it would have made him a martyr for his cause. He also said that if he were executed, he would still be considered a martyr. NBC News reported this week that the firing squad idea was set in motion this year inside the Pentagon, according to two U.S. officials familiar with the planning. President Donald Trump recently approved Hegseth’s recommendation to carry it out, chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said on social media. In his interview with Real America’s Voice, Hegseth was asked if he knew whether Hasan had contacted Trump or made any final requests. “Don’t care,” Hegseth said. “We’ll see him on Dec. 3rd.” According to the Death Penalty Information Center, after a president approves the death sentence from a case in a military court, the service member can seek habeas relief from the federal court system. If the habeas petition is ultimately denied, the servicemember, according to the center, would be led from death row down a flight of stairs to the United States Disciplinary Barracks’s death chamber where the servicemember would — traditionally — be strapped to a gurney and executed by lethal injection. The Defense Department, however, has said Hasan will be executed by firing squad. Hasan has represented himself throughout the yearslong legal process, though he had two lawyers with the U.S. Army Trial Defense Service who assisted as needed. It’s not clear at the moment whether he will appeal his method of execution.

articles.title: Dem who ripped rival’s donor-fueled 'good life' dropped campaign cash on Disney, spouse travel
articles.summary: Rep. Vicente Gonzalez, D-Texas, accused a GOP rival of "living the good life" on donor money, but his campaign reported nearly $20,000 spent on trips to Disney World, the UAE and Europe
articles.body: A House Democrat accused a Republican rival of "living the good life" on donor money after her campaign reported Disney World spending, and she was allegedly seen returning from the theme park around the same time. But Democratic Texas Rep. Vicente Gonzalez's own records show nearly $20,000 in campaign spending around the same time on international and domestic trips with his wife, including his own visit to Disney World, a five-star hotel stay on the beach in the UAE and a Michelin-starred restaurant bill in Zurich. Gonzalez made the jab at Republican Mayra Flores in October 2025, months after posting photos documenting his own two-day Disney World trip with his wife and several other associates on social media in April. The social media posts coincided with payments Gonzalez's campaign made to the Florida theme park and resort around the same time, totaling more than $1,100. PROMINENT DEM’S FATAL ERROR PROMPTS REPUBLICAN TO PREDICT ‘RED TIDAL WAVE’ IN BLUE STRONGHOLD The Disney payments and photos were just one piece of a broader travel and hospitality spending trail from Gonzalez’s campaign reviewed by Fox News Digital. His campaign reported thousands of dollars in expenses at upscale restaurants and hotels from Washington and Texas, to California and Europe, alongside campaign spending on multiple overseas trips during which Gonzalez's wife accompanied, or appeared to accompany, the congressman, according to posts Gonzalez shared on social media. During one 2024 trip to the UAE that utilized campaign funds and coincided with social media posts in the same location posted on Gonzalez's Facebook, more than $13,000 in airfare and hotel expenses were spent. Gonzalez described apparent photos of the trip on social media as an "after campaign break," and his posts showed the congressman with his wife doing various sightseeing activities and one photo from a bed inside a top-floor luxury hotel room next to the beach. The fifth-term Democrat representative is fighting to hold his South Texas seat against Republican Eric Flores in November after the GOP candidate defeated Mayra Flores and a crowded Republican field earlier this year. The race has drawn national attention as both parties battle for the district and Gonzalez enters the final stretch with a significant campaign cash advantage. Gonzalez took aim at rival Mayra Flores in 2025, suggesting she was potentially using campaign funds to travel to Disney World with her kids. In an October 2025 social media post, Gonzalez shared a photo of her at Dallas Love Field Airport with two young family members, a Disney World bag and stuffed animals. Gonzalez captioned the photo "living the good life on donor's resources again" and cited a report that found payments to Disney World from her campaign around the same time as the photos. But federal campaign finance records show Gonzalez's own campaign reported a combined $1,122.76 went to Walt Disney Resorts on March 24, 2025, and May 27, 2025, around the same time he posted photos on social media from a two-day trip to Walt Disney World with his own family on April 26, 2025. "DC to Disney! What a fantastic 2 days," Gonzalez posted on Facebook alongside a photo of himself, his wife and several others. SWALWELL PAL ACCUSED OF USING CAMPAIGN CASH TO BANKROLL ‘LUXURY LIFESTYLE,' INCLUDING SUPER BOWL TICKETS Federal campaign finance rules do not prohibit campaigns from paying travel expenses simply because a candidate's spouse or children accompany them. The FEC allows campaign funds to cover travel for candidates, their spouses and minor children when the trip is directly related to campaign activity or the candidate's official responsibilities as a federal officeholder. Campaign funds cannot, however, be used to pay for personal vacations or other family expenses that would have existed regardless of the candidate's campaign or official duties. When a trip mixes campaign or official business with personal activities, the campaign must be reimbursed for the costs attributable to the personal portion. "Every dollar this campaign spends is legal and publicly disclosed, and these reports come straight from our own FEC filings," Gonzalez's campaign manager, Alex Philley, told Fox News Digital in a statement when asked about the campaign spending. "The spending South Texans are worried about is their own on higher costs driven by Trump's agenda that Eric Flores would proudly rubber-stamp." Gonzalez's FEC filings identify two $561.38 Disney payments, one from March 2025 and another from May 2025, only as "travel expenses," leaving unclear from the public disclosures what campaign or official activity the expenditures were connected to. When asked specifically about this trip, Philley said it was tied to "a very important Financial Services trip" with Rep. French Hill, R-Ark., the Republican chairman of the U.S. House Committee on Financial Services, of which Gonzalez is a member. Philley said the campaign's spending on international trips where Gonzalez's wife was present had been tied to official business as well, including a visit with the Pope, although he did not address each trip separately when asked about them. SUPREME COURT STRIKES DOWN LIMIT ON PARTY CAMPAIGN SPENDING IN COORDINATION WITH CANDIDATES For example, Gonzalez traveled with his wife to Morocco in mid-2019 under the Mutual Educational and Cultural Exchange Act, or MECEA, which allows members of Congress to accept travel from foreign governments for approved cultural exchanges. Campaigns are allowed to pay for their spouses to join them, but only if the spouse is performing bona fide official responsibilities. Diplomatic and ceremonial protocol for certain events or campaign office functions like managing travel logistics are often cited as reasons for why spouses need to attend. Gonzalez's campaign reported paying $4,767.53 for his "spouse travel expense" in connection with the 2019 MECEA trip to Morocco, according to FEC records. In December 2024, the campaign reported $12,810 to Emirates Airlines and $359.27 at a luxury five-star Abu Dhabi hotel called Emirates Towers in "officially connected" CODEL expenses. While the campaign funds for the trip did not explicitly name Gonzalez’s wife, photos from Gonzalez's social media page showed several images of him and his wife in Abu Dhabi around the same time as his campaign's payments, including a photo from the top floor of what appeared to be a luxury, beachfront hotel. The pair also appeared in photos exploring the city and sightseeing around the time of the payments. SQUAD DEM IN THE HOT SEAT AFTER SPENDING SPREE AT LUXURY HOTELS: 'CHAMPAGNE SOCIALIST' "Finally, an after campaign break!" Gonzalez captioned the photos, one of which showed him holding an exotic bird. Other photos posted around that time by Gonzalez's campaign page showed him visiting U.S. troops in the Middle East and meeting with other officials. Other photos showed Gonzalez and his wife at the "4th largest and most modern Mosque in the world" in Abu Dhabi. The international travel continued in August 2025, when Gonzalez posted a photo with his wife in Zurich, Switzerland. Campaign records subsequently showed a $566.67 expense to Swiss Air and another $395 "Travel Expense" at La Rôtisserie in Zurich, a one-Michelin-star restaurant. The records did not explicitly indicate the expenses were used to pay for Gonzalez’s wife. Weeks earlier, Gonzalez appeared to engage in international luxury travel paid for by his campaign. FEC records for Gonzalez's campaign reveal a $442.41 "Travel Expense" at the five-star luxury Parco dei Principi Grand Hotel in Rome the same week he posted a photo of himself on social media meeting with the Pope in 2025. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "This was not a vacation," Philley said in a statement to Fox News Digital about the trip. "You may want to ask the committee why they booked this hotel. This was not the congressman’s choice; he only had to pay for it." Between 2024 and 2026, Gonzalez's campaign also reported thousands of dollars in expenditures at upscale restaurants, hotels and resorts around the country, including around $4,000 at The Capital Grille in Washington, D.C., along with spending at Eddie V's Prime Seafood in Houston and several other high-end D.C. restaurants. Recently, Gonzalez's campaign reported a $1,019 expense at California's Ojai Valley Inn, a Forbes Travel Guide-recognized luxury resort sprawling across 220 acres with a spa, four pools and a championship-caliber golf course and more than $1,400 at Pennsylvania's Omni Bedford Springs Resort & Spa, an AAA Four Diamond property featuring a 30,000-square-foot spa, golf course and indoor and outdoor pools.

articles.body:
The Trump administration on Thursday announced it would exempt some Arctic oil and gas exploration activities from environmental reviews.

© David W. Houseknecht, U.S. Geological Survey via Associated Press

The Interior Department issued a notice exempting wintertime oil and gas exploration in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska from the reviews.

The exemption will apply to seismic surveys to assess where oil is located, construction of temporary roads and drilling of exploration wells. These activities are often pursued in preparation for broader-scale oil production.

The administration says that its action could ultimately help oil companies access fuel more quickly. It also said that in the past, it has found that such activities would not have a significant environmental impact.

Bureau of Land Management Alaska State Director Kevin Pendergast said in a written statement that it would “allow developers to more nimbly locate energy resources in the Petroleum Reserve, ultimately increasing domestic energy supply, leading to stable energy costs and more revenue for Alaskan communities and the American public.”

However, environmental activists criticized the maneuver.

“In issuing this categorical exclusion, this administration is seeking to fast track large scale oil drilling and seismic exploration without any further environmental analysis or public input,” said Earthjustice Attorney Janet Bering in a written statement. “It is cutting the public out of this decision and future decisions.”

The move comes after the administration also recently proposed to fast-track oil production in the reserve.

articles.title: Hegseth says firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter will be ‘public’
articles.summary: An official at the Pentagon told Al Jazeera that former US Army Major Nidal Hasan’s execution would be ‘livestreamed’.
articles.body:
United States Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said the execution of a former US Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in Texas will be publicly available to watch.

In an interview with the media outlet Real America’s Voice on Thursday, Hegseth was asked about President Donald Trump’s recent order to use a firing squad to execute Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of the 2009 shooting.

The secretary said he approved of the decision, calling it a “no-brainer”.

“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public,” Hegseth told interviewer Jack Posobiec. “Because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”

Hegseth added that the execution would take place at Fort Hood on December 3 at 1pm US Central Time (19:00 GMT), the same time that the 2009 shooting took place.

Hasan was sentenced to death in August 2013 after a military jury found him guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted murder for the shooting.

The former Army major walked into an army processing centre on the Texas base, shouted “Allahu akbar” (God is greatest) and opened fire on fellow military members waiting to get medical attention.

Hasan’s execution required approval from Hegseth and Trump, who authorised the use of the firing squad on Monday.

An official with the Defense Department told Al Jazeera that Hasan’s execution would be “livestreamed”, adding that more details would come soon.

It is not clear from Hegseth’s remarks whether troops, spectators or US military officials would be present in person for the execution. US Army regulation states that at least two media outlets should be selected as witnesses.

No state or federal execution has ever been televised in the US. The last public execution in the country took place more than 90 years ago in Owensboro, Kentucky, on August 14, 1936.

The last time a US military execution was conducted by firing squad was in 1945, for desertion during World War II.

When asked to comment on Hegseth’s remarks – and whether Trump would view the execution – the White House referred Al Jazeera to the Pentagon.

The Trump administration announced it would add death by firing squad as an acceptable method for federal executions in April, along with gas asphyxiation and electrocution.

articles.title: Man shot by ICE in New York City
articles.summary: An Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent shot and wounded man in New York City Thursday evening, Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) confirmed. The New York Police Department (NYPD) first reported that a shooting “involving federal law enforcement agents” occurred at approximately 4 p.m. in the Bronx’s Marble Hill neighborhood, clarifying that city police were not…
articles.body:
An Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent shot and wounded man in New York City Thursday evening, Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) confirmed.

The New York Police Department (NYPD) first reported that a shooting “involving federal law enforcement agents” occurred at approximately 4 p.m. in the Bronx’s Marble Hill neighborhood, clarifying that city police were not involved in the incident. Officials confirmed to The Hill’s broadcasting partner NewsNation at around 6 p.m. that ICE agents were involved.

The officials told NewsNation that the victim was an illegal immigrant with a criminal record.

It is unknown how many officers were involved in the shooting at this time, according to federal law enforcement. The man was transported to a nearby hospital, the NYPD stated.

Mamdani posted to social platform X to denounce ICE’s actions in the city, with the mayor calling it “an incredibly serious situation.” He added that has already called President Trump about the incident.

“I have called the President; when we speak I will demand that he ends all ICE enforcement actions in our city,” he wrote. “I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorize our communities.”

The mayor said early reports indicated ICE agents fired multiple rounds at the victim’s car while he and his 5-year-old child were inside. The child was reportedly unharmed.

New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin echoed Mamdani’s stance on ICE’s alleged actions, saying she is “deeply troubled” by the reports.

“Federal authorities must provide us with a fully transparent account of what took place without delay,” Menin wrote. “I recognize the immense fear that ICE’s actions have caused immigrant New Yorkers, and I’m deeply worried about the additional anxiety and uncertainty this incident may bring to communities across our city as we await answers.”

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said she has been briefed on the shooting, and expects “a full and transparent accounting of the circumstances surrounding this incident,” she wrote on X.

The Bronx ICE-involved shooting comes less than a month after ICE agents similarly shot a Venezuelan national in Austin while he was delivering food. The man, 28, has since been charged with assault.

Despite some Democrats’ calls for the agency’s abolition, White House border czar Tom Homan has emphasized in recent weeks that ICE is “not going anywhere.”

After receiving the email, the station alerted law enforcement, prompting an investigation into the threat. FLORIDA MAN ARRESTED FOR ALLEGEDLY THREATENING TO KILL TRUMP, RUBIO AND BONDI Authorities said they later identified Hicks as the alleged sender of the email. "We must take threats of violence like this one seriously," U.S. Attorney Timothy Courchaine said in a statement. "I am grateful to our local news station for referring this threat to law enforcement, and to the FBI for addressing the situation quickly, professionally, and with the level of commitment it required," Courchaine added. According to federal officials, investigators also discovered additional email drafts in the account linked to Hicks. OHIO MAN CHARGED OVER GRAPHIC THREATS TO KILL TRUMP, BEHEAD GOP LAWMAKER Officials said the drafts, also dated Sept. 23, were addressed to other news organizations and contained similar threats involving the White House and other locations in Washington, D.C. The FBI is leading the investigation with assistance from the U.S. Secret Service. FBI Phoenix Special Agent in Charge Rebecca Day credited the news station for alerting authorities to the threat. "We appreciate the community partner who reported the threat to law enforcement. Cooperation and partnership are essential to protecting the American people," Day said.
